summary: Defines Q-Block1 and Q-Block2, alternative CoAP block-wise transfer options that complement the Block1 and Block2 options of RFC 7959. They support sending large data using Non-confirmable messages with fewer packet exchanges and allow faster recovery when blocks are lost.

eli5.summary: A big file is sent in small pieces without waiting for a reply after each one, and only missing pieces get resent.

questions: send large payloads over coap non-confirmable
how does coap recover lost blocks
subtitle: Block-wise transfer for CoAP that works with Non-confirmable messages, so large data can flow without a reply to every block.

tldr.problem: CoAP's block-wise transfer (Block1 and Block2) works in lock step with Confirmable messages, which breaks down when packet loss is asymmetrical, such as during a DDoS attack that floods the pipe.
tldr.mechanism: The Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 options let a sender push a whole set of blocks in Non-confirmable messages, while the receiver reports every missing block in one message and the sender resends only those.
tldr.outcome: Sending large bodies takes fewer packet exchanges and recovers faster from loss. The options complement Block1 and Block2 rather than replacing them, and they come with extra congestion control rules and a strong recommendation against the NoSec mode.

today: RFC 9177 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sits alongside RFC 7959, which defines the Block1 and Block2 options it complements.

sections.title: Why Block-Wise Transfer Needed a Rework
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) normally runs over UDP and recommends that a message fit in a single IP packet. RFC 7959 added the Block1 and Block2 options so that bigger data could be split into blocks. Those options work only with Confirmable (CON) messages, and they run in lock step: the next block can be sent or requested only when the previous one has completed, so the pace is set by round-trip times.

That is a poor fit when packet loss is asymmetrical, for example when acknowledgments get dropped. The RFC's example is a network under a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, where DDoS mitigation agents using CoAP still need to talk to each other. RFC 7959 recommends CON responses for loss, but that does not work with a flooded pipe.

RFC 9177 therefore introduces Q-Block1 and Q-Block2, which allow block-wise transfer with a series of Non-confirmable (NON) messages. A whole body can be sent without waiting for intermediate acknowledgments, and recovery is available if it is needed. The options are strictly layered on top of the base CoAP specification and remove none of its constraints.
sections.eli5: The old way is like asking permission after every single sentence you say. When the line is bad, replies get lost and everything stalls. The new way lets you say a lot at once and fix only the parts that got lost.

sections.title: Benefits, Costs and Where to Use It
sections.content:
Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 are similar in operation to Block1 and Block2, but they are not a replacement. The RFC lists these benefits: they work where packet loss is highly asymmetrical, they send sets of blocks with fewer packet interchanges, they recover faster from lost blocks, and they can send a whole body in NON messages without any intermediate response.

The costs are listed just as plainly. Blocks may arrive out of order, since lock-stepping is lost. NON messages need extra congestion control. Mixing NON and CON in one exchange is not supported, stateless operation and random access are not supported, proxying is limited to caching full representations, and there is no multicast support.

The primary target is applications such as DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) that cannot use CON because of potential packet loss. The RFC also notes that there is little benefit when CoAP runs over a reliable connection, because CON and NON are not used there. If a peer does not support the new options, transmissions can fall back to Block1 and Block2.

Using the options outside their primary use case should be weighed against a possible loss of interoperability with generic CoAP applications.
sections.eli5: It is a special tool for bad network days, not a replacement for your everyday tool. It gives up neat ordering to get more done when replies keep getting lost.

sections.title: The Q-Block Options
sections.content:
Q-Block1 (option number 19) pertains to the request payload, and Q-Block2 (option number 31) pertains to the response payload. Both are critical and unsafe to forward. Q-Block2 is also repeatable, but only when requesting retransmission of missing blocks. The option value uses the same structure as RFC 7959: a block number (NUM), a more bit (M) and a block size (SZX).

An endpoint or proxy MUST support either both options or neither. Because a critical option that is not understood may be silently ignored or answered with a Reset in a NON message, a client MUST use a Confirmable message to find out whether the peer supports them. A CON request that is not understood gets a 4.02 (Bad Option) response.

For the sending side, Q-Block1 requires a Request-Tag option, which MUST be the same for every request carrying one body and unique for each different body. The matching Q-Block2 rule is that every payload of one body MUST carry the same ETag. Q-Block1 requests MUST carry Size1, and Q-Block2 responses MUST carry Size2, each with the exact size of the body and the same value in every payload.

Block and Q-Block options must not be mixed in the same packet. With OSCORE, Q-Block options may appear as Inner or Outer options, and Block and Q-Block options may be mixed only across Inner and Outer.
sections.eli5: Every postcard carries a number and a sticker saying which letter it belongs to. The receiver uses those to put the letter back together, even if the postcards arrive in a jumbled order.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Blocks
sections.content:
With Q-Block1, the client sends payloads in order of increasing block number, starting from zero. For NON, the server does not have to answer until it has the whole body or a timer expires with some payloads missing. A 2.04 (Changed) or similar success code means the whole body arrived. A 2.31 (Continue) code says a full MAX_PAYLOADS_SET arrived and the client may go on. A 4.08 (Request Entity Incomplete) response carrying a special content type lists the missing blocks, and the client resends exactly those with the same Request-Tag, Size1 and block values. Duplicate blocks are ignored, but the server still responds as if the block was new.

With Q-Block2, the meaning of the M bit in a request depends on NUM. With M unset, the request is for that one block. With NUM zero and M set, it is a request for the entire body. With NUM a multiple of MAX_PAYLOADS and M set, it is the Continue request that confirms the previous set arrived and invites the server to send the next one. Any other NUM with M set asks for that block and the rest of the current set. Missing blocks are requested with several Q-Block2 options in ascending order and without duplicates, and the server sends each block only once to prevent amplification.

Servers SHOULD keep a cached copy of the body to answer retransmission requests. If the resource changes, the server uses a new ETag, and the client should treat the partial body with the old ETag as stale. Servers MUST ignore multicast requests that carry Q-Block2. For Observe, the Observe value must be the same in all payloads of one body, but a request for a missing payload must not include it.
sections.eli5: The sender fires off a batch of numbered pages. The receiver says either "got them all, send more" or "I am missing pages 1 and 9". The sender then resends only those pages.

sections.title: The Missing Blocks Message
sections.content:
A 4.08 (Request Entity Incomplete) response whose Content-Format is application/missing-blocks+cbor-seq tells the client that the server has not received all blocks it needs. The client must not treat it as a fatal error. Likely causes include blocks that were dropped, blocks the client has not sent yet, or blocks that were sent so long ago that the server discarded them.

The payload is a Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Sequence of one or more missing block numbers, each a CBOR unsigned integer. Numbers MUST be unique and in ascending order. The Content-Format option MUST be set to the new media type. If the list would not fit in a single packet, the server limits the report and sends the rest in later 4.08 responses when the client sends a new request for a missing payload with the same Request-Tag.

The response should reuse the token from the last block received with that Request-Tag, which lets the client find the original request and its Request-Tag. This response SHOULD NOT be used with Confirmable requests or reliable connections, because the client can see directly which payload failed.
sections.eli5: It is a short note that just lists page numbers, like "missing: 1, 9". Because it is only a list of numbers, it is tiny and easy to send.

sections.title: Congestion Control for NON Transfers
sections.content:
All blocks of one body over an unreliable transport MUST be either all CON or all NON. For CON, NSTART would need to be raised above 1 for speed, and the RFC leaves that tuning out of scope. For NON, the RFC adds new parameters and rules that MUST be followed in addition to the base CoAP congestion control.

A sender sends at most MAX_PAYLOADS blocks (default 10) at a time. This group is a MAX_PAYLOADS_SET. After each set, the sender waits for a random delay, NON_TIMEOUT_RANDOM, before the next set, unless the peer sends a Continue, in which case the next set MAY start at once. A receiver that is missing a block waits NON_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT before asking again, and the wait doubles on each retry. After NON_MAX_RETRANSMIT attempts the receiver SHOULD give up, discard the partial body and release its tokens.

The RFC works out an example: with 1500-byte packets and 10 payloads per set, each set is 120 kbits, and a 2 second delay between sets means an average of 60 kbps for one body if no responses arrive. That rate is further reduced by PROBING_RATE, which applies to a whole body rather than to single packets.
sections.eli5: If everyone shouted all their pages at once, the road would jam. So the sender sends ten pages, takes a short rest, and sends ten more, unless the other side says "go ahead" early.

sections.title: Proxies, Caching and Security
sections.content:
For simplicity, a proxy is expected to reassemble the whole body before passing it onward, using the recovery options if needed. The onward link need not use Q-Block, so a proxy that supports the options must fully support both. The Q-Block options are removed as part of assembly, and the ETag and Request-Tag are not part of the cache key. If a requested body is not in the cache, the proxy MUST request the entire body from the server.

On security, the RFC says it is NOT RECOMMENDED to use the NoSec mode with either option, with or without OSCORE. Even with OSCORE, an intermediary can modify the unprotected Outer Q-Block options to make a transfer fail or to keep requesting all blocks by setting the M bit, which causes attack amplification. The RFC also points readers to the security considerations of RFC 7959, RFC 7252 and RFC 9175.

IANA registered option numbers 19 (Q-Block1) and 31 (Q-Block2), the media type application/missing-blocks+cbor-seq, and CoAP Content-Format ID 272 for it.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle can mess with the numbered stickers and make the sender resend everything over and over. So the document tells you to use proper protection and not leave the line open.

items.label: Continue
items.desc: All blocks of the current MAX_PAYLOADS_SET arrived; send the next set. Only for NON.

items.label: Changed
items.desc: The entire body was received and the resource was updated.

items.label: Created
items.desc: The entire body was received and the resource was created.

items.label: Request Entity Incomplete
items.desc: With the missing-blocks content type, lists payloads to resend.

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: Q-Block1 was used without a Request-Tag or Size1 option.

items.label: Bad Option
items.desc: A Confirmable request used Q-Block options the server does not support.
